name: One tenant's long context evicts every other tenant's KV cache: a single request can consume more KV than hundreds of short ones, so a quota on request count does not protect anyone
symptom: A small number of users sending long-context requests degrades the service for everyone: their p50 latency is fine while other tenants' p50 and p99 climb sharply, and the other tenants' requests are the ones being preempted and re-prefilled (see ops-kv-cache-full-preempts-and-recomputes). No tenant has exceeded their quota. Fair-share metrics show one program with enormous average wait time and the rest collapsing. The escalation is always 'their request rate is fine', and it is: their request rate is not the problem.
root_cause: Capacity is consumed per token, not per request, and the engines' own victim selection is length-biased against long-prompt requests. llm-d names both halves: 'A single tenant sending massive prompts can monopolize an endpoint's KV cache and queue, starving others' and 'A single request with a massive context can consume more resources than hundreds of short requests.' SGLang's default --retraction-policy makes it explicit — 'length preserves the existing behavior and retracts short-output, long-input requests first' — so under KV pressure the engine preferentially sacrifices exactly the requests long-context tenants are sending. Compounding this, prefix caching makes cache residency a function of traffic history: a tenant with a hot shared prefix keeps a large slice of the cache permanently occupied, so its cost is invisible in both the request rate and the KV utilisation gauge of the moment.
workaround: Isolate at the routing layer with per-tenant fairness rather than hoping the engine shares fairly: llm-d Flow Control keys every request on a FlowKey of (FairnessID, Priority) with FairnessID extracted from the x-llm-d-inference-fairness-id header, and the round-robin fairness policy 'Guarantees fair sharing by cycling through active flows one by one ... Prevent[s] a single high-volume flow from starving others (solving the "Noisy Neighbor" problem)'. Add per-band memory isolation so a lower-priority tenant cannot consume the queue reserved for higher-priority ones — the global-strict policy deliberately does the opposite, 'Ignores flow isolation and serves all requests in a single global order'. Inside the engine, bound the worst case: cap max_model_len per tenant class, use max_num_seqs, and enable priority scheduling with a non-default retraction policy so eviction order is by priority rather than by length. Monitor fairness explicitly: llm_d_epp_program_aware_jains_fairness_index measures Jain's fairness over average wait time across active programs, with program_aware_avg_wait_time_milliseconds per program. Add cost to the quota itself (ops-ratelimit-token-vs-request-count).
notes: Upstream does not claim to have solved this: the Gateway API Inference Extension roadmap still lists 'Fairness and priority between workloads within the same criticality band' as future work. And Flow Control is behind a feature gate, so the mitigation is opt-in infrastructure, not something a stock llm-d install provides. One further honest gap: Flow Control 'cannot remove wait time when the system is over capacity' — it redistributes it between tenants, so in a genuinely undersized pool fairness makes everyone slow instead of making anyone fast. SCHEME RECLASSIFIED (2026-10-04): was 'config'.
